newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss form task forces to probe Holocaust accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss form task forces to probe Holocaust accounts.

text.p: Switzerland said on Wednesday it would form two task forces to probe mounting accusations that the unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims from Eastern Europe was used to compensate Swiss citizens for nationalised property.

"We want to clear up completely this important and painful matter as quickly as possible," Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti told reporters in announcing the new expert panels, but he made clear that thoroughness was more important than speed.

Cotti would not confirm that Swiss citizens who lost property in communist nationalisations were compensated in part from such unclaimed wealth, as suggested by previously secret documents now emerging from archives.
"I only can confirm that the federal council (cabinet) would like to make a very deep examination of the situation within a very short time," Cotti told Reuters.

One new task force will study compensation agreements Switzerland struck with then-communist regimes in eastern Europe. The other will review revelations now coming to light and try to build bridges to its foreign critics.
Switzerland has struggled to deal with a drumbeat of criticism from Jewish groups and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato about the way it handled dormant accounts of Holocaust victims.

Critics gained fresh ammunition from a study showing the Swiss paid Poland around 480,000 Swiss francs (now $382,800) and earmarked 325,000 francs for Hungary under secret deals that Jewish groups say robbed Holocaust victims of their wealth.
Swiss historian Peter Hug's research, published in a Zurich newspaper, showed a 1949 deal with Poland using Poles' unclaimed wealth to help settle Swiss claims was not an isolated deal.

"Switzerland made similar concessions to Hungary as it had to Poland," according to Hug's report, which was submitted to the foreign ministry in September but only emerged on Wednesday, when it was published in the Neue Zuercher Zeitung.

Berne agreed in 1950 to help Budapest, which like Poland was eager to get its hands on hard currency, search for dormant Swiss assets of Hungarians who died in the war, Hug said. He put the amount of money involved at 460,500 francs.

When the government in 1973 sought parliament's approval for a compensation treaty with Hungary, he added, it did not mention a confidential annexe that credited Budapest with 325,000 francs from unclaimed Holocaust accounts to be used for the payments.

In Poland's case, Switzerland gave Warsaw 16,347 francs in 1960 and another 463,955 francs in 1975 under the 1949 pact that used unclaimed wealth from dead Poles' bank accounts and life insurance policies to help pay Swiss for nationalised property.
This was less than the two million francs mentioned in other documents from the period that are now coming to light.
"Despite several Polish requests, Switzerland refused (in 1975) to give Polish authorities the names of the people originally entitled to the funds," Hug added.
"Thus even if Poland had wanted to, it would have been impossible to identify and pay survivors entitled to the funds."
The leader of Switzerland's Jewish community, Rolf Bloch, said the money should be returned to the orignial owners' heirs or turned over to charity.

"We demand...a quick determination of the facts and of the amount of the money involved and that these be given to the heirs or to the fund set up by federal decree in 1962 to distribute dormant assets to charitable organisations," he said.
